name: Trichloroacetic acid peel

lead: TCA peels use trichloroacetic acid to injure and renew the skin and are classed as medium-depth. They are used by clinicians for photodamage, pigment problems, acne and scars.
Published human studies exist but are mostly small.

paras: TCA is a strong acid that precipitates skin proteins, causing controlled injury; depth depends on concentration and technique.
ECHA lists severe skin burns and eye damage. Peel complications include prolonged redness, pigment changes, scarring and thinning. Wikipedia says medium peels must be done by a medical provider.

lead: A trichloroacetic acid (TCA) peel is a chemical peel using TCA, a strong acid, to cause controlled injury and shedding of the skin; it is described as a medium-depth peel usually done in a doctor's office or outpatient surgery centre.[1][2] It is used for photodamage, pigment disorders such as melasma, acne and scars, and actinic keratoses.[3][4][5]

Published trials are mostly small. Reports describe TCA compared with ascorbic acid combinations in melasma, with 5-ALA photodynamic therapy in actinic keratosis, and as part of combination peels.[4][6][7] Risks include pigment changes, scarring and prolonged redness.[2]
infobox: Severe skin burns and eye damage (ECHA)[1]

paras: TCA is a strong acid (pKa 0.66) that precipitates proteins and is used in chemical peels, tattoo removal and wart treatment.[1] Wikipedia states medium peels must be performed by a medical provider, that TCA peels cause warmth or burning, and that patients often receive pain relief.[2] The depth and effect vary with concentration and technique; one 1994 paper describes using glycolic acid before 35% TCA to make penetration more predictable.[8]

Studies have applied TCA to melasma,[4] actinic keratosis and skin cancer prophylaxis,[3][5] benign pigmented lesions in dark-skinned patients,[9] molluscum contagiosum in immunocompromised patients,[10] and acne and scars in registered trials.[11]

The European Chemicals Agency says TCA causes severe skin burns and eye damage.[1] Wikipedia lists photosensitivity, prolonged redness, hyperpigmentation, milia, skin thinning and texture changes among peel complications and warns that skin injury and scarring can occur.[2]

A randomised 5-year trial in 34 veterans examined facial resurfacing for actinic keratoses and new skin cancers.[3] A comparative study in 30 women with epidermal melasma compared 20% TCA alone to TCA plus topical 5% ascorbic acid.[4] A randomised trial compared 35% TCA with 5-ALA photodynamic therapy for multiple actinic keratosis.[5] A pilot study of three men examined collagen changes after a single 35% TCA peel.[6] Registered trials have compared TCA with salicylic acid for acne and with Jessner's solution for melasma.[7][11]
